status: Introduction, F, E and Lambda reviewed; Phi next
summary: QFEP asks who may revise the terms. Introduction keeps different arrangements with a similar total; F changes a prediction while its bits stay fixed; E closes and reopens branches; Lambda now moves a glowing recommendation while leaving the surrounding spectrum unchanged. Four laboratory halls have received this pass. Seven of eight declared halls remain authored; Sandbox is still to restore.

items.title: The outline remembers what the total cannot
items.description: KEEP retains one arrangement while you move the four controls. A pale outline stays beside the current coloured shape, and the readout shows the retained total and difference. The diagram can disagree while the number agrees.
captions: Keep A: F 0.4, E 0.2, lambda 0.5, phi 0.5. Total 0.450.
Change to B: F 0.6, E 0.6. Total 0.450 again; A remains as a pale outline.

items.before: Move one control on the workbench and watch both the numerical result and the shape of the four-axis display. Then try changing another control to return the result towards its earlier value. Look for two configurations that look different on the axes but give nearly the same total.
items.after:
Move one control on the workbench and watch both the numerical result and the shape of the four-axis display. Press KEEP. A pale outline holds that arrangement while your next movements redraw the coloured shape.

Now try changing two controls to return the result towards the kept total. Look for two configurations that look different on the axes but give nearly the same number. The outline remembers what the total cannot.

items.title: A handle can move without changing this total
items.description: The chapter’s existing zero-weight experiment stays. With lambda at zero, the E vertex moves but its contribution to the total is zero. The saved shape makes the movement visible. The controls also state their domains; the colour names a nearest authored example rather than a detected physical phase.
captions: Lambda zero, E 0.1. Keep this arrangement: total 0.550.
Lambda still zero, E 0.9. Another shape; total still 0.550.
items.image_note: The unchanged total is a property of this expression. It does not establish that entropy or change has disappeared from the surrounding room.
items.text_kind: book — names and ranges belong to particular instruments
items.before: The named phase on the display is selected by comparing the knob arrangement with authored reference configurations. A changing name therefore reports proximity to a project example; it does not announce an experimentally detected physical phase transition.
items.after:
All four rails on this console run from zero to one. Its phi is a nonnegative weight; the separate phi rail nearby, and the later Phi hall, also allow negative values. A familiar symbol does not guarantee the same range. Read the rail as well as the letter.

The display says “nearest project reference.” Its name and colour come from comparing your arrangement with seven authored examples. A name can change while you are still moving the same four handles. Watch when it changes: the border between two reference examples is a choice made in the comparison, not an experimentally detected physical phase transition.

items.title: F Term: same uncertainty, whose mistake?
items.description: A fixed seed gives 256 stored draws. Changing p re-thresholds them. EXPECT 0 marks each one as a miss. The entropy curve gives the same height at p=0.1 and p=0.9; this particular predictor does very differently. The main chapter’s proposed experiment now exists in the museum.
captions: p=0.1, EXPECT 0: source H≈0.469; 27 observed misses in 256 cells.
p=0.9, EXPECT 0: source H≈0.469; 230 observed misses in 256 cells.
items.image_note: Same camera, actual Godot museum. Amber underlines mark errors in the displayed sample. Expected percentages and observed counts are shown separately. H is a source quantity, not the measured encoding length of this grid.
items.text_kind: book — the proposed predictor becomes an encounter
items.before: Imagine a predictor that always expects zero. It would usually succeed near one end of the rail and usually fail near the other, although the entropy can be the same at those two settings. The example separates uncertainty in a source from mismatch between a source and a particular predictor.
items.after: Press EXPECT 0. Each amber underline marks a bit that refuses that guess. Compare p near 0.1 with p near 0.9 again. The entropy returns to almost the same height, but the mistakes spread. The source is no more uncertain; this predictor is less suited to it.

items.title: Improve the prediction without changing the world
items.description: Keep p at 0.9 and press EXPECT 1. The bit colours and positions stay fixed. Their amber marks change sides, and observed misses fall from 230 to 26. This is an explicit mismatch count for a simple predictor; the screen does not claim to measure variational free energy.
captions: EXPECT 0: 230 misses. The source and sample are held fixed for the next image.
EXPECT 1: 26 misses. The same bits meet a different expectation.
items.image_note: 26 runtime assertions and five selected walking routes pass. 70 content/preservation checks pass. This tests the control signals and calculations in the museum, not tracked hands or learner understanding.
items.text_kind: book — the critical question grows from the comparison
items.before: The next useful addition would display that predictor’s expectations and errors beside the grid. It could then change its expectations while the source stays fixed. A learner would see whether improvement came from an easier world or from a better model of it.
items.after:
Leave p near 0.9 and press EXPECT 1. Keep your eye on the bits, not only the number. Their colours stay; the amber marks change sides. You have improved this predictor’s performance without making the world easier.

The screen distinguishes expected errors under the chosen probability from mistakes counted in this particular grid. They need not agree exactly. The smaller experiment is enough to ask something consequential: when we call a world difficult, whose expectation is meeting it?

Here you can change the expectation with one button. Elsewhere a system might insist that the world change instead. Keep that difference with you.

items.title: What QFEP means — from the project documents
items.description: QFEP means Queer Free Energy Principle. The research notes ask that a model’s terms remain revisable while what it leaves out retains the capacity to act. Self-Q brings the question back to the maker and the museum: what do our own structures teach us to notice? The introduction now includes both, with document footnotes. The reading note links the sources and separates the ethical proposal from the teaching arithmetic.
items.text_kind: Introduction — the project’s definition enters the book
items.before: This is an operational introduction to the project’s QFEP expression, QFE = F − λE(S) + φΔE(S,t). F names a modelling or free-energy contribution, E an entropy contribution, lambda their relative weighting, and phi the weighting attached to change. The console lets you inspect that arithmetic. It does not measure these quantities from a living system, and its fixed change value is not an observed rate.
items.after:
QFEP stands for **Queer Free Energy Principle**. Ada uses the name to ask something of a model as well as something through it: whose persistence does it support, which differences can it notice, and who may change its terms? In the project’s research documents, Q keeps those terms open to revision while protecting the capacities of what the model leaves out to live, act and answer back. More entropy is not, by itself, more freedom. A boundary can shelter a body; opening it can also expose that body to harm.[^qfep]

The documents call the return of this question to the maker **Self-Q**. A structure teaches its maker what to notice next. After enough time with these four rails, we may begin looking only for things that fit them. What have they made thinkable? What have they made harder to think? What continues beyond their reach? The museum must be able to ask this of its own rooms, including this one.[^self-q]
items.report_label: Read the QFEP definition and source guide

items.title: E Term: a closure has consequences upstream of the count
items.description: OPEN holds 81 endings. PRUNE closes 18 branches at the third level, removing 54 later endings and leaving 27. Amber caps mark where continuation stops. The existing pruned prospect is now visitor-selectable. The gallery retains its seven placed works, with a level approach and side passages.
captions: OPEN: 81 leaves; H≈4.39 nats under equal leaf weights.
PRUNE: 27 leaves; 18 branch closures remove 54 endings.
items.image_note: Same camera, actual Godot museum. Thinner branches and separated leaf markers make the count visible. The fan assumes equal weights; it does not measure visits or moral value.
items.text_kind: E Term — the proposed extension becomes an encounter
items.before:
Now choose a branch and imagine it being closed. Distinguish an option that was available and then prohibited from an option never drawn at all. A picture of the permitted future can hide the history of how the permissions were chosen. Counting its leaves cannot recover those omitted alternatives.

For a proposed extension, let visitors mark one closed path and preserve its outline. The fan could then show both the current count and the choices excluded from it, instead of making absence look inevitable.
items.after:
Press PRUNE. Amber caps appear where branches stop. The fan has twenty-seven leaves now, where OPEN offered eighty-one. Eighteen closures remove fifty-four endings: a cut made earlier takes several later possibilities with it. Follow one of the amber stops. You can see where continuation was refused, even though the missing subtree is no longer drawn.

This is where QFEP’s Q reaches into the diagram. Who drew the tree? Who can request another branch, or refuse the condition for reaching it? The project’s research documents ask that what a model leaves out retain the capacity to challenge and change its terms.[^q] Our four buttons still belong to a tree someone else specified. You can reopen it. You cannot yet ask it to grow otherwise.

items.title: Reopening is easy here. Changing the rule is still another question.
items.description: OPEN restores the same authored fan. It does not let a visitor invent a new kind of ending, and it models none of the losses that real closure can leave behind. The chapter keeps that limit as an invitation. A protective boundary may sustain a vulnerable body; counting more leaves cannot decide what care requires.
captions: A visible stop carries the trace of an excluded continuation.
The same 81 endings return at a button press.
items.image_note: 31 runtime checks, five selected walking routes and 78 content/preservation checks pass. Headset reach, reading comfort and learner understanding remain pending. A pre-existing secondary microstate-counter formatting error is recorded for follow-up.
items.text_kind: E Term — an easy reset meets a harder question
items.before: For a proposed extension, let visitors mark one closed path and preserve its outline. The fan could then show both the current count and the choices excluded from it, instead of making absence look inevitable.
items.after:
Press OPEN again. Here the same endings return at a touch. Outside this little machine, reopening a route may not restore the lives or histories lost when it closed. The ease of the button is part of the experiment’s limit.

Keeping every branch open is not automatically care. A closure might protect a place in which a more vulnerable body can continue. The count cannot decide that for us. Stay with the difference between more endings on a screen and more ways to live.

items.title: Lambda: the light moves; the forms keep their places
items.description: A new entrance rail moves only the lit floor strip and its inscriptions. The repeated cubes, dispersed forms, row colours and animation settings do not follow. The original authored preference remains visible in the way the rows stand aside and take on green. A suggestion can change while its inherited conditions stay in place.
captions: Suggested λ=0.20: the light lies towards the repeated side.
Suggested λ=0.80: the light lies beneath the more dispersed forms.
items.image_note: Same camera and held animation instant in the actual Godot museum. Runtime assertions compare every row/wall MultiMesh buffer, material emphasis and drifter transform before and after the control signal. Normal animation remains independent and was checked separately.
items.text_kind: book — the existing proposed experiment becomes an action
items.before: For a future comparison, move the lit route while keeping the structures fixed. Would a group’s preferred position change? That experiment would examine the architecture’s influence separately from the numerical vocabulary used to describe it.
items.after:
Return to the small console at the entrance. Move LIT STRIP. The light slides across the floor; the rows do not follow. Their colours keep their earlier emphasis and the moving forms continue their own motion. Try a recommendation near each end of the rail, then press RETURN. Which invitation did you find easiest to believe?

Watch for disagreement. The bright strip may now point beneath a form instead of through the gap the architecture prepared. Light has made a recommendation, not cleared a passage. The rail moves between 0.20 and 0.80 to keep its strip inside the hall’s kerbs; even this power to recommend has been given a limit.

items.title: Two invitations now occupy the same room
items.description: RETURN restores the first recommendation without reseeding or rearranging the spectrum. The chapter’s opening and main argument are preserved exactly. Its addition asks what else a visitor would need to change before this felt like their decision. The full-size hall is now centred inside a larger gallery, and its map placements override an older stamp that omitted it.
captions: RETURN: the lit strip again agrees with the gap prepared for it.
LIT STRIP and RETURN at the entrance to the full-size hall.
items.image_note: 28 interaction/state checks, six selected walking routes and 71 content checks pass. The rendered process saved its report and all five images, then crashed on shutdown. An independent headless run on the final source passes and exits 0. Headset comfort and visitor preference remain unverified.
items.text_kind: book — the QFEP question follows the action
items.before: The entropy fan asked which alternatives were available. The hall adds another question: which available alternatives are made inviting? A pathway, colour or rhythm can recommend an answer before any explanatory text does.
items.after:
There are two kinds of preference visible now: the one you can move, and the one already built into the rows. Changing the sign does not erase the arrangement that made the first invitation convincing. Would another visitor choose differently after seeing your version first?

QFEP asks who may revise a model’s terms. Here you can change one of the room’s terms of persuasion. Its forms, its colours and the possibilities on the rail remain authored. What else would you need to change before this felt like your decision?
